records.source: וְיִפְתָּ֣ח הַגִּלְעָדִ֗י הָיָה֙ גִּבּ֣וֹר חַ֔יִל וְה֖וּא בֶּן־אִשָּׁ֣ה זוֹנָ֑ה וַיּ֥וֹלֶד גִּלְעָ֖ד אֶת־יִפְתָּֽח׃
records.gloss: And Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty [man] of strength, and he [was the] son of a woman, a prostitute; and fathered Gilead Jephthah.
pieces: Jephthah the Gileadite was a strong warrior. He was the son of a prostitute, and his father was Gilead.

L.1: And Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of strength, and he [was the] son of a woman [who was] a prostitute; and Gilead fathered Jephthah.

R.1: Jephthah from Gilead was a brave and strong fighter. His mother was a prostitute, and his father was a man named Gilead.

decisions.choice: a mighty man of strength: a proven fighting man
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of Gideon (6:12) and of men able to fight (2 Kings 24:14). It names a man known for courage and skill in war; it may also suggest a man of some standing, but here the story makes him a fighter first.

decisions.choice: son of a woman, a prostitute: born outside his father's marriage
decisions.reason: Jephthah's mother was not Gilead's wife but a prostitute. This gives him no rightful place in the family, as the next verse shows, and it puts him among the unlikely leaders the book tells of.

decisions.choice: Gilead fathered Jephthah: a man named Gilead
decisions.reason: Gilead is also the name of the region and of a clan of Manasseh (Numbers 26:29). Here it names Jephthah's father. The name may show how closely the man and his family belonged to the land and people of Gilead.

decisions.choice: a man named Gilead
decisions.reason: Readable adds "a man named" so the reader does not confuse the father with the region of Gilead in the same sentence.

records.heading: Jephthah the Gileadite

records.source: וַתֵּ֧לֶד אֵֽשֶׁת־גִּלְעָ֛ד ל֖וֹ בָּנִ֑ים וַיִּגְדְּל֨וּ בְֽנֵי־הָאִשָּׁ֜ה וַיְגָרְשׁ֣וּ אֶת־יִפְתָּ֗ח וַיֹּ֤אמְרוּ לוֹ֙ לֹֽא־תִנְחַ֣ל בְּבֵית־אָבִ֔ינוּ כִּ֛י בֶּן־אִשָּׁ֥ה אַחֶ֖רֶת אָֽתָּה׃
records.gloss: And bore the wife of Gilead to him sons, and grew up the sons of the wife, and they drove out Jephthah and said to him, not you will inherit in [the] house of our father, for [the] son of a woman another [are] you.
pieces: Gilead's wife also bore him sons. When they grew up, they drove Jephthah away and told him, "You will have no share in our father's estate, because you are the son of another woman."

L.2: And the wife of Gilead bore him sons, and the sons of the wife grew up, and they drove Jephthah out and said to him, "You will not inherit in the house of our father, for you [are the] son of another woman."

R.2: Gilead's wife had sons too. When they grew up, they forced Jephthah to leave. They said, "You will not get any of our father's property. You are the son of a different woman."

decisions.choice: not inherit in our father's house: no share in the family's land and goods
decisions.reason: The "house of our father" is the family and what it owns. The sons of Gilead's wife shut out the son of the prostitute from any share. The law protected a firstborn son of a less loved wife (Deuteronomy 21:15-17), but a prostitute's son had no such claim; Sarah similarly wanted Hagar's son shut out of the inheritance (Genesis 21:10).

decisions.choice: drove out: forced him to leave by pressure or force
decisions.reason: The verb is used of driving people out of a place they had lived in. Jephthah later says the elders of Gilead shared in this (verse 7).

decisions.choice: our father's estate / our father's property
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "inherit in the house of our father" means; Literal keeps the phrase.

records.source: וַיִּבְרַ֤ח יִפְתָּח֙ מִפְּנֵ֣י אֶחָ֔יו וַיֵּ֖שֶׁב בְּאֶ֣רֶץ ט֑וֹב וַיִּֽתְלַקְּט֤וּ אֶל־יִפְתָּח֙ אֲנָשִׁ֣ים רֵיקִ֔ים וַיֵּצְא֖וּ עִמּֽוֹ׃פ
records.gloss: And fled Jephthah from [the] face of his brothers and dwelt in [the] land of Tob; and gathered themselves to Jephthah men empty, and they went out with him.
pieces: So Jephthah escaped from his brothers and made his home in the land of Tob. A band of worthless men gathered around him and went out raiding with him.

L.3: And Jephthah fled from the presence of his brothers and lived in the land of Tob; and empty men gathered themselves to Jephthah, and they went out with him.

R.3: So Jephthah ran away from his brothers and went to live in the land of Tob. A gang of rough men with nothing to lose joined him, and they went out on raids together.

decisions.choice: the land of Tob: a region north and east of Gilead
decisions.reason: Tob lay beyond Israel's settled land, toward Aram. Later the Ammonites hire men from Tob against David (2 Samuel 10:6, 8).

decisions.choice: empty men: men without land, means or standing
decisions.reason: "Empty" men are men with nothing to their name, ready for any risk. Abimelech hired the same kind of men (9:4), and David later gathers a similar band (1 Samuel 22:2).

decisions.choice: went out with him: went out on raids
decisions.reason: "Go out" is often used of going out to fight. With a band of such men, it most likely means raiding, which explains how Jephthah gained the fighting skill the elders want.

decisions.choice: went out raiding / went out on raids
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state the most likely sense of "went out" (m3). Literal keeps the bare verb.

records.source: וַיְהִ֖י מִיָּמִ֑ים וַיִּלָּחֲמ֥וּ בְנֵֽי־עַמּ֖וֹן עִם־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And it was after days, and fought [the] sons of Ammon with Israel.
pieces: Some time later the Ammonites went to war against Israel.

L.4: And it was after [some] days, and the sons of Ammon fought with Israel.

R.4: After some time, the Ammonites started a war against Israel.

decisions.choice: after days: after some time
decisions.reason: The phrase sets no exact length of time. The story goes back to the war already begun in 10:17.

records.source: וַיְהִ֕י כַּאֲשֶׁר־נִלְחֲמ֥וּ בְנֵֽי־עַמּ֖וֹן עִם־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיֵּֽלְכוּ֙ זִקְנֵ֣י גִלְעָ֔ד לָקַ֥חַת אֶת־יִפְתָּ֖ח מֵאֶ֥רֶץ טֽוֹב׃
records.gloss: And it was when fought [the] sons of Ammon with Israel, and went [the] elders of Gilead to fetch Jephthah from [the] land of Tob.
pieces: When the Ammonites were fighting against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah back from the land of Tob.

L.5: And it was, when the sons of Ammon fought with Israel, that the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob.

R.5: So while the Ammonites were at war with Israel, the leaders of Gilead went to the land of Tob to get Jephthah.

decisions.choice: the elders of Gilead: the heads of the families and towns of the region
decisions.reason: Elders were the older men who led families and towns and spoke for them. These are the leaders who had asked who would lead the fight against Ammon (10:18).

decisions.choice: leaders
decisions.reason: Readable says "leaders" for "elders" here, because the point is their office, not their age.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ לְיִפְתָּ֔ח לְכָ֕ה וְהָיִ֥יתָה לָּ֖נוּ לְקָצִ֑ין וְנִֽלָּחֲמָ֖ה בִּבְנֵ֥י עַמּֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And they said to Jephthah, come and be to us for commander, and let us fight against [the] sons of Ammon.
pieces: They said to Jephthah, "Come and be our commander, so that we can fight the Ammonites."

L.6: And they said to Jephthah, "Come and be our commander, and let us fight against the sons of Ammon."

R.6: They said to Jephthah, "Come and lead our army, so that we can fight the Ammonites."

decisions.choice: commander: a leader in war only
decisions.reason: The word names a military chief. The elders first offer Jephthah command of the army for this war. In verse 8 they raise the offer to "head" over all the people of Gilead, and in verse 11 he is made both.

decisions.choice: let us fight: so that we may fight
decisions.reason: The verb expresses what the elders want to do once Jephthah leads them; it gives the purpose of their request.

decisions.choice: lead our army
decisions.reason: Readable says what a commander does, so the step up to "head" in verse 8 stays clear.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יִפְתָּח֙ לְזִקְנֵ֣י גִלְעָ֔ד הֲלֹ֤א אַתֶּם֙ שְׂנֵאתֶ֣ם אוֹתִ֔י וַתְּגָרְשׁ֖וּנִי מִבֵּ֣ית אָבִ֑י וּמַדּ֜וּעַ בָּאתֶ֤ם אֵלַי֙ עַ֔תָּה כַּאֲשֶׁ֖ר צַ֥ר לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And said Jephthah to [the] elders of Gilead, [did] not you hate me and drive me out from [the] house of my father? And why have you come to me now, when distress [is] to you?
pieces: But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Was it not you who hated me and drove me out of my father's house? Why come to me now, when you are in trouble?"

L.7: And Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Did you not hate me and drive me out of the house of my father? And why have you come to me now, when you are in distress?"

R.7: But Jephthah answered the leaders of Gilead, "You hated me and forced me to leave my father's home! So why are you coming to me now that you are in trouble?"

decisions.choice: did not you hate me: a question that accuses
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer yes. The pronoun "you" is stressed: Jephthah lays the blame on the elders themselves, not only on his brothers, perhaps because they supported or allowed his expulsion.

decisions.choice: when distress is to you: only now that you need me
decisions.reason: Jephthah points out that they turn to him only in need. The LORD had said much the same to Israel in 10:13-14: you left me, so cry to the gods you chose. Jephthah's bargaining follows.

decisions.choice: statement with an exclamation mark
decisions.reason: Readable turns the first question into the statement it implies, so its force is not missed.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְרוּ֩ זִקְנֵ֨י גִלְעָ֜ד אֶל־יִפְתָּ֗ח לָכֵן֙ עַתָּה֙ שַׁ֣בְנוּ אֵלֶ֔יךָ וְהָלַכְתָּ֣ עִמָּ֔נוּ וְנִלְחַמְתָּ֖ בִּבְנֵ֣י עַמּ֑וֹן וְהָיִ֤יתָ לָּ֨נוּ֙ לְרֹ֔אשׁ לְכֹ֖ל יֹשְׁבֵ֥י גִלְעָֽד׃
records.gloss: And said [the] elders of Gilead to Jephthah, therefore now we have returned to you, and you will go with us and fight against [the] sons of Ammon, and you will be to us for head of all [the] inhabitants of Gilead.
pieces: The elders of Gilead answered Jephthah, "That is exactly why we have come back to you now. Come with us and fight the Ammonites, and you will be our head, ruling over everyone who lives in Gilead."

L.8: And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we have now come back to you: you will go with us and fight against the sons of Ammon, and you will be head over us, over all the inhabitants of Gilead."

R.8: The leaders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "Yes, that is why we have come back to you now. Come with us and fight the Ammonites. Then you will be the ruler over all of us who live in Gilead."

decisions.choice: therefore: that is why, because we are in distress
decisions.reason: The word picks up Jephthah's complaint and turns it: yes, it is because of the trouble that we have come. It does not deny what he said about the past.

decisions.choice: head of all the inhabitants of Gilead: ruler of the whole region
decisions.reason: "Head" is more than "commander" (verse 6): it means lasting rule over all Gilead, not only command in this war. It is what the leaders had promised in 10:18 to whoever began the fight against Ammon.

decisions.choice: Come with us
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "and you will go with us" sets out the terms; Balanced and Readable put it as an invitation, which is how it works in the talk.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יִפְתָּ֜ח אֶל־זִקְנֵ֣י גִלְעָ֗ד אִם־מְשִׁיבִ֨ים אַתֶּ֤ם אוֹתִי֙ לְהִלָּחֵם֙ בִּבְנֵ֣י עַמּ֔וֹן וְנָתַ֧ן יְהוָ֛ה אוֹתָ֖ם לְפָנָ֑י אָנֹכִ֕י אֶהְיֶ֥ה לָכֶ֖ם לְרֹֽאשׁ׃
records.gloss: And said Jephthah to [the] elders of Gilead, if bringing back you me to fight against [the] sons of Ammon, and gives Yahweh them before me, I will be to you for head.
pieces: Jephthah answered the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me back to make war on the Ammonites and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} hands them over to me, then I will be your head."

L.9: And Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me back to fight against the sons of Ammon, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gives them up before me, I will be your head."

R.9: Jephthah said to the leaders of Gilead, "Suppose you take me back to fight the Ammonites, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lets me defeat them. Then I will be your ruler. Agreed?"

decisions.choice: I will be your head: a condition set as a statement
decisions.reason: Jephthah restates the elders' offer as his own terms, with the pronoun "I" stressed. The words could also be read as a question ("will I really be your head?"), but either way he wants the promise made firm, as the elders do in verse 10.

decisions.choice: the LORD gives them before me: victory comes from the LORD
decisions.reason: Jephthah speaks of victory as the LORD's gift, as the book does throughout (3:10; 4:14; 7:9). He names the LORD as the one who decides the war, before any vow is made.

decisions.choice: Agreed?
decisions.reason: Readable adds "Agreed?" to show that Jephthah is pinning the elders down, which their oath in verse 10 answers. It is a stretch beyond the words.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ זִקְנֵֽי־גִלְעָ֖ד אֶל־יִפְתָּ֑ח יְהוָ֗ה יִהְיֶ֤ה שֹׁמֵ֨עַ֙ בֵּֽינוֹתֵ֔ינוּ אִם־לֹ֥א כִדְבָרְךָ֖ כֵּ֥ן נַעֲשֶֽׂה׃
records.gloss: And said [the] elders of Gilead to Jephthah, Yahweh will be hearing between us, if not according to your word so we do.
pieces: The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "{{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is witness between us. We will certainly do as you say."

L.10: And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "{{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will be the one who hears between us, if we do not do just as you say."

R.10: The leaders of Gilead answered, "{{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is listening and is our witness. We promise to do just what you have said."

decisions.choice: the LORD will be the one hearing between us: the LORD is witness to this agreement
decisions.reason: The elders call on the LORD to hear their promise and hold them to it. Laban uses a similar oath with Jacob (Genesis 31:49-50).

decisions.choice: if we do not do according to your word: a solemn oath, meaning we will surely do it
decisions.reason: An oath in Hebrew often begins "if ..." and leaves the curse unspoken: may the LORD act against us if we fail. It amounts to a firm promise.

decisions.choice: We will certainly do as you say / We promise to do
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn the oath form "if we do not do" into the promise it makes (m2).

records.source: וַיֵּ֤לֶךְ יִפְתָּח֙ עִם־זִקְנֵ֣י גִלְעָ֔ד וַיָּשִׂ֨ימוּ הָעָ֥ם אוֹת֛וֹ עֲלֵיהֶ֖ם לְרֹ֣אשׁ וּלְקָצִ֑ין וַיְדַבֵּ֨ר יִפְתָּ֧ח אֶת־כָּל־דְּבָרָ֛יו לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה בַּמִּצְפָּֽה׃פ
records.gloss: And went Jephthah with [the] elders of Gilead, and made the people him over them for head and for commander; and spoke Jephthah all his words before Yahweh in Mizpah.
pieces: So Jephthah went back with the elders of Gilead, and the people set him over themselves as head and commander. And Jephthah repeated all his terms before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} at Mizpah.

L.11: And Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head over them and commander; and Jephthah spoke all his words before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} in Mizpah.

R.11: So Jephthah went back with the leaders of Gilead. The people made him their ruler and the commander of their army. Then at Mizpah, Jephthah repeated everything he had agreed to, there in the presence of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: head and commander: both offers given together
decisions.reason: The people give Jephthah both titles: lasting rule (verse 8) and command in war (verse 6).

decisions.choice: spoke all his words before the LORD: the agreement made binding at a place of worship
decisions.reason: Speaking the terms "before the LORD" made the agreement a sacred one, with the LORD as witness (verse 10). Mizpah in Gilead was where Israel had gathered against Ammon (10:17).

decisions.choice: repeated all his terms / repeated everything he had agreed to
decisions.reason: "All his words" here are the terms just agreed; Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח יִפְתָּח֙ מַלְאָכִ֔ים אֶל־מֶ֥לֶךְ בְּנֵֽי־עַמּ֖וֹן לֵאמֹ֑ר מַה־לִּ֣י וָלָ֔ךְ כִּֽי־בָ֥אתָ אֵלַ֖י לְהִלָּחֵ֥ם בְּאַרְצִֽי׃
records.gloss: And sent Jephthah messengers to [the] king of [the] sons of Ammon, saying, what [is] to me and to you, that you have come to me to fight against my land?
pieces: Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites with this question: "What quarrel do you have with me, that you have come to attack my land?"

L.12: And Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the sons of Ammon, saying, "What [is there] between me and you, that you have come to me to fight against my land?"

R.12: Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites. They asked him, "What do you have against me? Why have you come to attack my country?"

decisions.choice: what is to me and to you?: what quarrel is there between us?
decisions.reason: The phrase asks what claim one side has on the other. Here it challenges the king to give a reason for his war (compare 2 Samuel 16:10; 1 Kings 17:18).

decisions.choice: my land: Jephthah speaks for Israel
decisions.reason: As head of Gilead, Jephthah speaks of Israel's land as his own, just as the king calls the disputed land "my land" (verse 13). The talks are between two rulers on behalf of their peoples.

decisions.choice: two questions
decisions.reason: Readable splits the question into two short ones.

records.heading: Jephthah's message to the king of Ammon

records.source: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ מֶ֨לֶךְ בְּנֵי־עַמּ֜וֹן אֶל־מַלְאֲכֵ֣י יִפְתָּ֗ח כִּֽי־לָקַ֨ח יִשְׂרָאֵ֤ל אֶת־אַרְצִי֙ בַּעֲלוֹת֣וֹ מִמִּצְרַ֔יִם מֵאַרְנ֥וֹן וְעַד־הַיַּבֹּ֖ק וְעַד־הַיַּרְדֵּ֑ן וְעַתָּ֕ה הָשִׁ֥יבָה אֶתְהֶ֖ן בְּשָׁלֽוֹם׃
records.gloss: And said [the] king of [the] sons of Ammon to [the] messengers of Jephthah, because took Israel my land when it came up from Egypt, from Arnon and to the Jabbok and to the Jordan; and now restore them in peace.
pieces: The king of the Ammonites answered Jephthah's messengers, "Because Israel took my land when they came up from Egypt, all the way from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan. Now give it back peacefully."

L.13: And the king of the sons of Ammon said to the messengers of Jephthah, "Because Israel took my land when it came up from Egypt, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan. And now give them back in peace."

R.13: The king of the Ammonites gave this answer to Jephthah's messengers: "When the Israelites came up out of Egypt, they took my land. It stretched from the Arnon River north to the Jabbok River and west to the Jordan River. Now give it back to me without a fight."

decisions.choice: from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan: the land Israel took from Sihon
decisions.reason: These are the bounds of the land Israel took from Sihon king of the Amorites (Numbers 21:24; verse 22 below). The king of Ammon claims it as his own. Numbers says Ammon's border lay beyond it to the east (Numbers 21:24).

decisions.choice: restore them: give back the lands, or the towns in them
decisions.reason: The word "them" is plural, though "land" is singular. It probably means the lands or towns within the bounds just named. The sense is the same: give back the whole area.

decisions.choice: in peace: without war
decisions.reason: The king offers to stop the war if the land is handed over. The words are a demand, not a request.

decisions.choice: it
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "it" for the plural "them", since English uses "land" as a whole (m2).

decisions.choice: River; north; west
decisions.reason: Readable adds "River" and the directions so that a reader can picture the area claimed.

records.source: וַיּ֥וֹסֶף ע֖וֹד יִפְתָּ֑ח וַיִּשְׁלַח֙ מַלְאָכִ֔ים אֶל־מֶ֖לֶךְ בְּנֵ֥י עַמּֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And again added Jephthah and sent messengers to [the] king of [the] sons of Ammon.
pieces: Jephthah sent messengers once more to the king of the Ammonites,

L.14: And Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the sons of Ammon,

R.14: So Jephthah sent messengers again to the king of the Ammonites.

decisions.choice: added again and sent: sent a second time
decisions.reason: "Add" with another verb means to do something again. Jephthah answers the king's claim with a longer message.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֔וֹ כֹּ֖ה אָמַ֣ר יִפְתָּ֑ח לֹֽא־לָקַ֤ח יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֶת־אֶ֣רֶץ מוֹאָ֔ב וְאֶת־אֶ֖רֶץ בְּנֵ֥י עַמּֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And he said to him, thus says Jephthah, not took Israel [the] land of Moab and [the] land of [the] sons of Ammon.
pieces: and they said to him, "This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites.

L.15: and he said to him, "Thus says Jephthah: Israel did not take the land of Moab or the land of the sons of Ammon.

R.15: They said to the king, "This is Jephthah's message: Israel did not take any land from the Moabites or from the Ammonites.

decisions.choice: Israel did not take the land of Moab or of Ammon: Israel kept the LORD's command
decisions.reason: The LORD told Israel not to attack Moab or Ammon or take their land, because he had given it to the descendants of Lot (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19). Jephthah's first point is that Israel obeyed.

decisions.choice: he said to him: the message spoken through the messengers
decisions.reason: The verb is singular, but the words are carried by the messengers. Jephthah's message runs from here to the end of verse 27.

decisions.choice: thus says Jephthah: the formula of a messenger
decisions.reason: A messenger began with the name of the one who sent him, then spoke in his name, using "I". Moses' message to Edom begins the same way (Numbers 20:14).

decisions.choice: they said
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "they" for the messengers, who actually speak (m2). Literal keeps the singular.

decisions.choice: a quotation opened and left open
decisions.reason: The message runs to verse 27, so its quotation marks open here and close there. The messages Israel sent long ago (verses 17 and 19) stand inside it with single quotation marks.

records.source: כִּ֖י בַּעֲלוֹתָ֣ם מִמִּצְרָ֑יִם וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֤ל בַּמִּדְבָּר֙ עַד־יַם־ס֔וּף וַיָּבֹ֖א קָדֵֽשָׁה׃
records.gloss: For when they came up from Egypt, and went Israel through the wilderness to [the] Sea of Reeds, and it came to Kadesh.
pieces: When Israel came up from Egypt, it journeyed through the wilderness as far as the Red Sea and then reached Kadesh.

L.16: For when they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Sea of Reeds and came to Kadesh.

R.16: When the Israelites came out of Egypt, they traveled through the desert to the Red Sea. Then they came to Kadesh.

decisions.choice: through the wilderness to the Sea of Reeds and to Kadesh: the journey told in Numbers
decisions.reason: Jephthah sums up Israel's wandering after the exodus: the way to the Sea of Reeds (Numbers 14:25) and the long stay at Kadesh (Numbers 20:1; Deuteronomy 1:46).

decisions.choice: the Sea of Reeds: the sea Israel crossed, and the gulfs to the south
decisions.reason: The name means "sea of reeds". It is used of the sea crossed in the exodus and of the gulfs on either side of the Sinai peninsula; here it is one stage of the wilderness journey.

decisions.choice: Red Sea
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the familiar name "Red Sea"; Literal keeps "Sea of Reeds", as in Numbers 21:4.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֣ח יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל מַלְאָכִ֣ים׀אֶל־מֶלֶךְ֩ אֱד֨וֹם׀לֵאמֹ֜ר אֶעְבְּרָה־נָּ֣א בְאַרְצֶ֗ךָ וְלֹ֤א שָׁמַע֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אֱד֔וֹם וְגַ֨ם אֶל־מֶ֧לֶךְ מוֹאָ֛ב שָׁלַ֖ח וְלֹ֣א אָבָ֑ה וַיֵּ֥שֶׁב יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בְּקָדֵֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: And sent Israel messengers to [the] king of Edom, saying, let me pass please through your land, and not listened [the] king of Edom; and also to [the] king of Moab it sent, and not he was willing; and stayed Israel in Kadesh.
pieces: Israel sent messengers to ask the king of Edom, 'Please allow us to cross your land.' But the king of Edom paid no attention. They sent the same request to the king of Moab, and he refused too. So Israel remained at Kadesh.

L.17: And Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, 'Please let me pass through your land'; but the king of Edom did not listen. And it also sent to the king of Moab, but he was not willing. So Israel stayed at Kadesh.

R.17: Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom. They asked, 'Please let us go through your country.' But the king of Edom would not listen. Israel sent the same message to the king of Moab, but he said no too. So the Israelites stayed at Kadesh.

decisions.choice: the request to the king of Edom: Numbers 20:14-21
decisions.reason: Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to ask Edom for passage, and Edom refused (Numbers 20:14-21). Jephthah's point is that Israel asked first and did not force its way.

decisions.choice: the request to the king of Moab: known only from this verse
decisions.reason: Numbers does not tell of a message to Moab, though Deuteronomy 2:29 mentions dealings with Moab on the way. Jephthah adds it to show that Israel asked both nations and was refused by both.

decisions.choice: let me pass: Israel speaks as one person
decisions.reason: The message uses "I" for the whole people, as Numbers 20:14-19 does.

decisions.choice: let us pass
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "us" for the people as a whole (m3).

records.source: וַיֵּ֣לֶךְ בַּמִּדְבָּ֗ר וַיָּ֜סָב אֶת־אֶ֤רֶץ אֱדוֹם֙ וְאֶת־אֶ֣רֶץ מוֹאָ֔ב וַיָּבֹ֤א מִמִּזְרַח־שֶׁ֨מֶשׁ֙ לְאֶ֣רֶץ מוֹאָ֔ב וַֽיַּחֲנ֖וּן בְּעֵ֣בֶר אַרְנ֑וֹן וְלֹא־בָ֨אוּ֙ בִּגְב֣וּל מוֹאָ֔ב כִּ֥י אַרְנ֖וֹן גְּב֥וּל מוֹאָֽב׃
records.gloss: And it went through the wilderness and went around [the] land of Edom and [the] land of Moab, and it came from [the] rising of [the] sun to [the] land of Moab, and they camped on [the] other side of Arnon; and not they came into [the] territory of Moab, for Arnon [was the] border of Moab.
pieces: Then Israel traveled through the wilderness and went around the lands of Edom and Moab. They passed along the east side of Moab and camped on the far side of the Arnon. They did not enter Moabite territory, because the Arnon was the border of Moab.

L.18: And it went through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab, and came to the east of the land of Moab, and they camped on the other side of the Arnon; but they did not come into the territory of Moab, for the Arnon [was] the border of Moab.

R.18: Then the Israelites went through the desert around the countries of Edom and Moab. They went along the east side of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon River. They did not go into Moab at all, because the Arnon River was Moab's border.

decisions.choice: around Edom and Moab, camped across the Arnon: Numbers 21:4, 10-13
decisions.reason: Israel went around Edom (Numbers 21:4) and along the edge of Moab, then camped beyond the Arnon, which Numbers 21:13 also calls the border of Moab.

decisions.choice: from the rising of the sun: on the east
decisions.reason: The place where the sun rises means the east. Israel kept to the desert side of Moab.

decisions.choice: the other side of the Arnon: north of the river
decisions.reason: The Arnon is a deep gorge flowing west into the Dead Sea. Moab lay south of it; the camp on its other side was in the land Sihon held (Numbers 21:13, 26).

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מַלְאָכִ֔ים אֶל־סִיח֥וֹן מֶֽלֶךְ־הָאֱמֹרִ֖י מֶ֣לֶךְ חֶשְׁבּ֑וֹן וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל נַעְבְּרָה־נָּ֥א בְאַרְצְךָ֖ עַד־מְקוֹמִֽי׃
records.gloss: And sent Israel messengers to Sihon king of the Amorite[s], king of Heshbon, and said to him Israel, let us pass please through your land to my place.
pieces: Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled at Heshbon, and said to him, 'Please allow us to cross your land to our own place.'

L.19: And Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, 'Please let us pass through your land to my place.'

R.19: Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon, the king of the Amorites, who ruled in the city of Heshbon. They said to him, 'Please let us go through your country to the land that is ours.'

decisions.choice: the request to Sihon: Numbers 21:21-22
decisions.reason: Israel asked Sihon for passage in the same way it had asked Edom (Numbers 21:21-22). Heshbon was his royal city (Numbers 21:26).

decisions.choice: my place: the land promised to Israel, west of the Jordan
decisions.reason: Israel asked only to pass through to the land the LORD had promised it beyond the Jordan. It did not want Sihon's land, Jephthah says; the war came from Sihon.

decisions.choice: our own place / the land that is ours
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "our" to match "us" earlier in the sentence; Literal keeps the shift from "us" to "my".

records.source: וְלֹא־הֶאֱמִ֨ין סִיח֤וֹן אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ עֲבֹ֣ר בִּגְבֻל֔וֹ וַיֶּאֱסֹ֤ף סִיחוֹן֙ אֶת־כָּל־עַמּ֔וֹ וַֽיַּחֲנ֖וּ בְּיָ֑הְצָה וַיִּלָּ֖חֶם עִם־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And not trusted Sihon Israel to pass through his territory, and gathered Sihon all his people and they camped at Jahaz, and he fought with Israel.
pieces: But Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory. He gathered all his forces, camped at Jahaz and attacked Israel.

L.20: But Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory; and Sihon gathered all his people, and they camped at Jahaz, and he fought with Israel.

R.20: But Sihon did not trust the Israelites to go peacefully through his land. So he called together his whole army. They set up camp at Jahaz, and he attacked Israel.

decisions.choice: did not trust Israel to pass: refused out of suspicion
alternatives: did not allow Israel to pass
decisions.reason: The verb means to believe or trust. Sihon did not believe Israel would pass through peacefully. Numbers 21:23 says only that he would not allow it; Jephthah gives the reason.

decisions.choice: gathered his people at Jahaz and fought: Numbers 21:23
decisions.reason: Jephthah follows Numbers 21:23: Sihon gathered his forces, came to Jahaz and fought Israel. The war was Sihon's doing.

decisions.choice: forces / army
decisions.reason: "His people" here are the men he called out to fight; Balanced and Readable say so, as Numbers 21:23 does.

records.source: וַ֠יִּתֵּן יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל אֶת־סִיח֧וֹן וְאֶת־כָּל־עַמּ֛וֹ בְּיַ֥ד יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וַיַּכּ֑וּם וַיִּירַשׁ֙ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֵ֚ת כָּל־אֶ֣רֶץ הָאֱמֹרִ֔י יוֹשֵׁ֖ב הָאָ֥רֶץ הַהִֽיא׃
records.gloss: And gave Yahweh God of Israel Sihon and all his people into [the] hand of Israel, and they struck them; and took possession Israel of all [the] land of the Amorite[s], who dwelt [in] that land.
pieces: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his forces into Israel's power, and Israel defeated them and took possession of the whole land of the Amorites who lived in that region.

L.21: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they struck them; and Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites, who lived in that land.

R.21: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, let the Israelites defeat Sihon and his whole army. So Israel took over all the land of the Amorites who lived there.

decisions.choice: the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon into Israel's hand: the victory was the LORD's
decisions.reason: Jephthah's argument rests on this: Israel did not take the land by its own choice, the LORD gave it (Numbers 21:34; Deuteronomy 2:31-33). The full title "the God of Israel" sets the LORD against the god of the Ammonite king (verse 24).

decisions.choice: took possession of: took over as its own
decisions.reason: The verb means to take land and hold it as an inheritance. It returns in verses 22-24, where it also means to drive out the people who held it.

decisions.choice: into Israel's power
decisions.reason: Balanced says "power" for the picture of "hand", as Judges does with this phrase; Literal keeps "hand", and Readable says what it meant.

records.source: וַיִּ֣ירְשׁ֔וּ אֵ֖ת כָּל־גְּב֣וּל הָאֱמֹרִ֑י מֵֽאַרְנוֹן֙ וְעַד־הַיַּבֹּ֔ק וּמִן־הַמִּדְבָּ֖ר וְעַד־הַיַּרְדֵּֽן׃
records.gloss: And they took possession of all [the] territory of the Amorite[s], from Arnon and to the Jabbok, and from the wilderness and to the Jordan.
pieces: They took over the whole Amorite territory, from the Arnon in the south to the Jabbok, and from the wilderness across to the Jordan.

L.22: And they took possession of all the territory of the Amorites, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and from the wilderness to the Jordan.

R.22: They took over all the land of the Amorites. It reached from the Arnon River north to the Jabbok River, and from the desert in the east to the Jordan River in the west.

decisions.choice: from the Arnon to the Jabbok, from the wilderness to the Jordan: the land of Sihon
decisions.reason: The same bounds as the king's claim (verse 13), with the east-west line added: the desert on the east, the Jordan on the west. Numbers 21:24 gives the north-south bounds. Jephthah's point is that this was Amorite land, not Ammonite.

decisions.choice: River; north; east; west
decisions.reason: Readable adds "River" and directions so that a reader can picture the area.

records.source: וְעַתָּ֞ה יְהוָ֣ה׀אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל הוֹרִישׁ֙ אֶת־הָ֣אֱמֹרִ֔י מִפְּנֵ֖י עַמּ֣וֹ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְאַתָּ֖ה תִּירָשֶֽׁנּוּ׃
records.gloss: And now Yahweh God of Israel has dispossessed the Amorite[s] from before his people Israel, and you will take possession of it?
pieces: So now that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, has driven out the Amorites before {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people Israel, are you to take their land?

L.23: And now {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, has dispossessed the Amorites from before {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people Israel, and you would take possession of it?

R.23: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, forced the Amorites out of their land to make room for {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people Israel. So do you think you can take that land now?

decisions.choice: has dispossessed: drove out the people who held the land
decisions.reason: The verb is the causative of "take possession" (verse 21): the LORD made the Amorites lose the land so that Israel could hold it. The same word ends this verse, so the question sets the LORD's act against the king's wish.

decisions.choice: and you will take possession of it?: a question that expects "no"
decisions.reason: There is no question word, but the stress on "you" makes it a scornful question: are you going to take what the LORD gave Israel?

decisions.choice: to make room for
decisions.reason: Readable says what "from before his people" means: the Amorites were driven out so that Israel could live there.

records.source: הֲלֹ֞א אֵ֣ת אֲשֶׁ֧ר יוֹרִֽישְׁךָ֛ כְּמ֥וֹשׁ אֱלֹהֶ֖יךָ אוֹת֥וֹ תִירָ֑שׁ וְאֵת֩ כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֨ר הוֹרִ֜ישׁ יְהוָ֧ה אֱלֹהֵ֛ינוּ מִפָּנֵ֖ינוּ אוֹת֥וֹ נִירָֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: [Is it] not that which causes you to possess Chemosh your god, it you will possess? And all that has dispossessed Yahweh our God from before us, it we will possess.
pieces: Do you not take possession of whatever your god Chemosh gives you? In the same way, we will possess all the land of those whom {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} our God has driven out before us.

L.24: Is it not [so that] whatever Chemosh your god gives you to possess, that you will possess? And all that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} our God has dispossessed from before us, that we will possess.

R.24: You keep whatever land your god Chemosh gives you, do you not? In the same way, we will keep all the land of the people that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} our God has driven out for us.

decisions.choice: Chemosh your god: the god of Moab
alternatives: Chemosh as a god worshiped in Ammon too
decisions.reason: Chemosh was the national god of Moab (Numbers 21:29; 1 Kings 11:7, 33); the god of Ammon was Milcom (1 Kings 11:5). Jephthah may name Chemosh because the land in dispute had once been Moab's (Numbers 21:26), or because the Ammonite king ruled Moabite land as well. The text does not say which.

decisions.choice: what Chemosh gives you: an argument on the king's own terms
decisions.reason: Jephthah reasons from what the king himself believes: you keep what you think your god gave you, so we keep what the LORD gave us. He does not grant that Chemosh is a true god; in verse 27 the LORD alone is the judge between the two peoples.

decisions.choice: is it not ...?: a question that expects "yes"
decisions.reason: The first half is a question the king must agree with; the second half draws the conclusion for Israel.

decisions.choice: all the land of those whom / of the people that
decisions.reason: "Dispossess" has people as its object; Balanced and Readable add "land" so that it is clear what Israel will possess.

records.source: וְעַתָּ֗ה הֲט֥וֹב טוֹב֙ אַתָּ֔ה מִבָּלָ֥ק בֶּן־צִפּ֖וֹר מֶ֣לֶךְ מוֹאָ֑ב הֲר֥וֹב רָב֙ עִם־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אִם־נִלְחֹ֥ם נִלְחַ֖ם בָּֽם׃
records.gloss: And now [are] really better you than Balak son of Zippor king of Moab? Did he really quarrel with Israel, or did he really fight against them?
pieces: Are you really a better man than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever dispute with Israel or make war on them?

L.25: And now, are you really better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever quarrel with Israel, or did he ever fight against them?

R.25: Do you think you are better than Balak son of Zippor, who was king of Moab? He never argued with Israel about the land, and he never went to war against them.

decisions.choice: Balak son of Zippor: the king of Moab who feared Israel
decisions.reason: Balak saw what Israel had done to the Amorites and hired Balaam to curse them (Numbers 22-24), but he never took the land back by war. Joshua 24:9 speaks of his hostility through Balaam; Jephthah's point is that he did not claim Sihon's land.

decisions.choice: really better ... did he really quarrel ... did he really fight: questions made stronger
decisions.reason: Each verb is doubled for stress. The questions all expect the answer "no".

decisions.choice: statements for the last two questions
decisions.reason: Readable gives the answer the questions expect, so the reader does not miss the point. It adds "about the land", the matter in dispute.

records.source: בְּשֶׁ֣בֶת יִ֠שְׂרָאֵל בְּחֶשְׁבּ֨וֹן וּבִבְנוֹתֶ֜יהָ וּבְעַרְע֣וֹר וּבִבְנוֹתֶ֗יהָ וּבְכָל־הֶֽעָרִים֙ אֲשֶׁר֙ עַל־יְדֵ֣י אַרְנ֔וֹן שְׁלֹ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת שָׁנָ֑ה וּמַדּ֥וּעַ לֹֽא־הִצַּלְתֶּ֖ם בָּעֵ֥ת הַהִֽיא׃
records.gloss: When dwelt Israel in Heshbon and in its daughters, and in Aroer and in its daughters, and in all the cities that [are] on [the] sides of Arnon, three hundred years, and why not did you recover [them] in that time?
pieces: Israel has lived in Heshbon and its villages, in Aroer and its villages, and in all the towns along the Arnon for 300 years. Why did you not take them back during all that time?

L.26: When Israel lived in Heshbon and in its daughters, and in Aroer and in its daughters, and in all the cities that [are] beside the Arnon, 300 years, why did you not recover [them] at that time?

R.26: Israel has lived for 300 years in Heshbon and Aroer and the villages around them, and in all the towns along the Arnon River. Why did you not take them back during all that time?

decisions.choice: its daughters: the villages that belonged to a town
decisions.reason: "Daughters" of a town are the smaller places around it that depended on it (Numbers 21:25).

decisions.choice: Heshbon, Aroer, the towns beside the Arnon: the land Israel settled
decisions.reason: Heshbon had been Sihon's royal city (Numbers 21:26). Aroer stood on the edge of the Arnon gorge (Deuteronomy 2:36). The "sides" (literally "hands") of the Arnon are its banks.

decisions.choice: 300 years: a round number for a very long time
decisions.reason: The years given in Judges 3-10 for times of oppression and peace add up to more than this, so the number fits as a round figure. Jephthah's point is that the claim comes far too late.

decisions.choice: villages
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "villages" for "daughters" (m1), as Numbers 21:25 does.

records.source: וְאָֽנֹכִי֙ לֹֽא־חָטָ֣אתִי לָ֔ךְ וְאַתָּ֞ה עֹשֶׂ֥ה אִתִּ֛י רָעָ֖ה לְהִלָּ֣חֶם בִּ֑י יִשְׁפֹּ֨ט יְהוָ֤ה הַשֹּׁפֵט֙ הַיּ֔וֹם בֵּ֚ין בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וּבֵ֖ין בְּנֵ֥י עַמּֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And I not have sinned against you, and you [are] doing with me evil by fighting against me; may judge Yahweh the Judge today between [the] sons of Israel and between [the] sons of Ammon.
pieces: I have not wronged you, but you are wronging me by making war on me. Let {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, who is the Judge, settle the case today between the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} and the Ammonites."

L.27: And I have not sinned against you, but you are doing me wrong by fighting against me. May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the Judge, judge today between the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel and the sons of Ammon."

R.27: I have done nothing wrong to you. But you are doing wrong to me by attacking me. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is the judge. Let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} decide today who is right, the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} or the Ammonites."

decisions.choice: sinned against you ... doing evil with me: wronged in a matter of right
decisions.reason: "Sin against" here means to wrong another party, as in a dispute between peoples (1 Samuel 24:12). Jephthah says the wrong is all on Ammon's side.

decisions.choice: the LORD, the Judge, judge: God settles the dispute
decisions.reason: This is the only place in Judges where the title "the judge" is given in the singular, and it is given to the LORD. The human judges lead and rescue; the LORD is the one who decides between the nations, as Abraham calls him "the Judge of all the earth" (Genesis 18:25). The battle will show his verdict.

decisions.choice: settle the case / decide
decisions.reason: "Judge" here means to decide a case, not to lead Israel, so Balanced says "settle the case" and Readable "decide"; the title "the Judge" stays.

decisions.choice: who is right
decisions.reason: Readable says what the LORD is asked to decide.

records.source: וְלֹ֣א שָׁמַ֔ע מֶ֖לֶךְ בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֑וֹן אֶל־דִּבְרֵ֣י יִפְתָּ֔ח אֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׁלַ֖ח אֵלָֽיו׃פ
records.gloss: And not listened [the] king of [the] sons of Ammon to [the] words of Jephthah that he sent to him.
pieces: But the king of the Ammonites paid no attention to the message Jephthah sent him.

L.28: But the king of the sons of Ammon did not listen to the words of Jephthah that he sent to him.

R.28: But the king of the Ammonites would not listen to Jephthah's message.

decisions.choice: did not listen: refused to accept the message
decisions.reason: "Listen" here means to heed. The king rejects Jephthah's case, and the matter goes to battle, where the LORD will judge (verse 27).

records.source: וַתְּהִ֤י עַל־יִפְתָּח֙ ר֣וּחַ יְהוָ֔ה וַיַּעֲבֹ֥ר אֶת־הַגִּלְעָ֖ד וְאֶת־מְנַשֶּׁ֑ה וַֽיַּעֲבֹר֙ אֶת־מִצְפֵּ֣ה גִלְעָ֔ד וּמִמִּצְפֵּ֣ה גִלְעָ֔ד עָבַ֖ר בְּנֵ֥י עַמּֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And was on Jephthah [the] Spirit of Yahweh, and he passed through the Gilead and Manasseh, and he passed through Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed on [to the] sons of Ammon.
pieces: Then the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came on Jephthah. He went through Gilead and Manasseh, passed through Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he went on against the Ammonites.

L.29: And the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came on Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, and passed through Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed on [to] the sons of Ammon.

R.29: Then the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came on Jephthah. He went through Gilead and Manasseh to gather an army. He passed through Mizpah in Gilead, and from there he went on to fight the Ammonites.

decisions.choice: the Spirit of the LORD came on Jephthah: the LORD equips him to lead
decisions.reason: As with Othniel (3:10) and Gideon (6:34), the Spirit gives the leader power to lead Israel to victory. The Spirit comes on Jephthah before he makes his vow (verses 30-31); the story does not say the LORD asked for a vow.

decisions.choice: passed through Gilead and Manasseh: gathering men for war
decisions.reason: Jephthah went through the lands of the eastern tribes, most likely calling out fighters, as Gideon did (6:35). Manasseh here is the half of the tribe settled east of the Jordan.

decisions.choice: passed on to the sons of Ammon: advanced against them
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has no word for "to"; the verb with the people as its object means he moved on against them.

decisions.choice: to gather an army
decisions.reason: Readable states the likely purpose of the journey (m2); the Hebrew does not say it outright.

records.heading: Jephthah makes a vow

records.source: וַיִּדַּ֨ר יִפְתָּ֥ח נֶ֛דֶר לַיהוָ֖ה וַיֹּאמַ֑ר אִם־נָת֥וֹן תִּתֵּ֛ן אֶת־בְּנֵ֥י עַמּ֖וֹן בְּיָדִֽי׃
records.gloss: And vowed Jephthah a vow to Yahweh and said, if indeed you give [the] sons of Ammon into my hand,
pieces: And Jephthah made a vow to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: "If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will truly hand the Ammonites over to me,

L.30: And Jephthah vowed a vow to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and said, "If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} indeed give the sons of Ammon into my hand,

R.30: Jephthah made a promise to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. He said, "If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will really let me defeat the Ammonites,

decisions.choice: if you indeed give them into my hand: a vow made before battle
decisions.reason: Israel made a vow in nearly the same words before fighting the king of Arad (Numbers 21:2). A vow was a promise to give God something if he granted a request (Genesis 28:20-22; 1 Samuel 1:11), and once made it had to be kept (Numbers 30:3; Deuteronomy 23:22-24).

decisions.choice: indeed give: the verb doubled for stress
decisions.reason: The repeated verb makes the condition strong: if you will surely give. It shows how much Jephthah wants the victory assured.

decisions.choice: the vow runs into verse 31
decisions.reason: The vow is one sentence across verses 30-31, so its quotation opens here and closes at the end of verse 31.

records.source: וְהָיָ֣ה הַיּוֹצֵ֗א אֲשֶׁ֨ר יֵצֵ֜א מִדַּלְתֵ֤י בֵיתִי֙ לִקְרָאתִ֔י בְּשׁוּבִ֥י בְשָׁל֖וֹם מִבְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֑וֹן וְהָיָה֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה וְהַעֲלִיתִ֖הוּ עוֹלָֽה׃פ
records.gloss: then it will be [that] the one coming out who comes out from [the] doors of my house to meet me in my returning in peace from [the] sons of Ammon, and it will be Yahweh's, and I will offer it up [as] a burnt offering.
pieces: then whoever or whatever comes out through the doors of my house to meet me as I come home safe from the Ammonites will be {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s, and I will sacrifice it as a burnt offering."

L.31: then the [one] coming out, that comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the sons of Ammon, shall be {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s, and I will offer it up [as] a burnt offering."

R.31: then when I come home safe from the battle, whoever or whatever comes out of my house first to meet me will belong to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I will offer it up as a burnt offering."

decisions.choice: the one coming out: whoever or whatever comes out, left open
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "the one coming out", a masculine form that Hebrew uses both for a person and for an animal or thing; it has no separate neuter. Some take Jephthah to mean a person: "to come out of the doors of my house to meet me" is what people do, and women came out to welcome a victor with song and dance (Exodus 15:20; 1 Samuel 18:6), as his daughter does in verse 34. Others take him to mean an animal: Israelite houses often sheltered animals on the ground floor, and a burnt offering was an animal (Leviticus 1). The words do not settle which he had in mind, so they are kept open.

decisions.choice: it will be the LORD's, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering: two parts of one promise
alternatives: it will be the LORD's, or I will offer it up as a burnt offering
decisions.reason: The plain sense is that what comes out will be given to the LORD by being offered as a burnt offering. Some read the second "and" as "or": it will belong to the LORD, or, if it is fit for sacrifice, be offered. That reading bears on verse 39, but "and" is the usual sense of the word.

decisions.choice: a burnt offering: an offering wholly burned on the altar
decisions.reason: A burnt offering was killed and burned whole for the LORD (Leviticus 1:9). The law strictly forbids offering people as sacrifices (Leviticus 18:21; 20:2-5; Deuteronomy 12:31; 18:10), and the LORD had not asked for this vow.

decisions.choice: when I return in peace: when I come back safe and victorious
decisions.reason: "In peace" means unharmed. For a war leader, coming home safe means coming home the winner.

decisions.choice: whoever or whatever comes out
decisions.reason: English has to choose between "whoever" and "whatever". Balanced and Readable name both so that they keep the question open as the Hebrew does (m1). Literal keeps "the [one] coming out".

decisions.choice: first
decisions.reason: Readable adds "first": the vow is about the one who comes out to meet him on his return, which means the first to reach him.

records.source: וַיַּעֲבֹ֥ר יִפְתָּ֛ח אֶל־בְּנֵ֥י עַמּ֖וֹן לְהִלָּ֣חֶם בָּ֑ם וַיִתְּנֵ֥םיְהוָ֖ה בְּיָדֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And passed on Jephthah to [the] sons of Ammon to fight against them, and gave them Yahweh into his hand.
pieces: So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight them, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} handed them over to him.

L.32: And Jephthah passed on to the sons of Ammon to fight against them, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave them into his hand.

R.32: Then Jephthah went to fight the Ammonites, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave him victory over them.

decisions.choice: the LORD gave them into his hand: the LORD grants the victory
decisions.reason: The words answer verse 9 and the vow's own condition (verse 30) in the same terms. The narrator says the LORD gave the victory; he does not say the vow won it.

decisions.choice: gave him victory over them
decisions.reason: Readable says what "gave them into his hand" means.

records.source: וַיַּכֵּ֡ם מֵעֲרוֹעֵר֩ וְעַד־בּוֹאֲךָ֨מִנִּ֜ית עֶשְׂרִ֣ים עִ֗יר וְעַד֙ אָבֵ֣ל כְּרָמִ֔ים מַכָּ֖ה גְּדוֹלָ֣ה מְאֹ֑ד וַיִּכָּֽנְעוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֔וֹן מִפְּנֵ֖י בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃פ
records.gloss: And he struck them from Aroer and until your coming [to] Minnith, twenty cities, and to Abel-keramim, a blow great very; and were humbled [the] sons of Ammon before [the] sons of Israel.
pieces: He defeated them with a great slaughter from Aroer to the area of Minnith, twenty towns, and as far as Abel-keramim. So the Ammonites were brought under the power of the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}.

L.33: And he struck them from Aroer until you come to Minnith, twenty cities, and as far as Abel-keramim, a very great blow. And the sons of Ammon were humbled before the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel.

R.33: He completely defeated them. He attacked twenty of their towns, from Aroer to near Minnith, and as far as Abel-keramim. So the Ammonites were brought under the control of the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}.

decisions.choice: Aroer, Minnith, Abel-keramim: towns toward the heart of Ammon
decisions.reason: Minnith and Abel-keramim ("meadow of vineyards") cannot now be located with certainty; they lay in or near Ammonite land. This Aroer may be the one "facing Rabbah", the Ammonite capital (Joshua 13:25), rather than the Aroer on the Arnon (verse 26).

decisions.choice: until your coming to Minnith: up to the approach to Minnith
decisions.reason: "Until you come to" is a way of marking the end of a route, as a traveler would describe it.

decisions.choice: the sons of Ammon were humbled: brought low, as earlier enemies were
decisions.reason: The same phrase ends the stories of Ehud (3:30), Deborah (4:23) and Gideon (8:28). The oppression begun in 10:7-9 is ended.

decisions.choice: were brought under the power / control of
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what being "humbled before" another people meant: losing power to them.

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֨א יִפְתָּ֣ח הַמִּצְפָּה֮ אֶל־בֵּיתוֹ֒ וְהִנֵּ֤ה בִתּוֹ֙ יֹצֵ֣את לִקְרָאת֔וֹ בְתֻפִּ֖ים וּבִמְחֹל֑וֹת וְרַק֙ הִ֣יא יְחִידָ֔ה אֵֽין־ל֥וֹ מִמֶּ֛נּוּ בֵּ֖ן אוֹ־בַֽת׃
records.gloss: And came Jephthah [to] Mizpah to his house, and look, his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and with dances; and only she [was] an only [child]; not was to him from him son or daughter.
pieces: When Jephthah reached his home in Mizpah, out came his daughter to meet him, dancing to the beat of tambourines. She was his one and only child; apart from her he had no son or daughter.

L.34: And Jephthah came to Mizpah, to his house, and look, his daughter [was] coming out to meet him with tambourines and with dancing; and she [was] his one and only [child]; besides her he had neither son nor daughter.

R.34: When Jephthah came back to his home in Mizpah, his daughter came out to meet him. She was playing a tambourine and dancing. She was his only child. He had no other sons or daughters.

decisions.choice: coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing: the welcome for a victor
decisions.reason: Women went out with drums and dancing to celebrate a victory (Exodus 15:20; 1 Samuel 18:6). The words "coming out to meet him" repeat the vow (verse 31): the reader sees at once who has come out.

decisions.choice: an only child: the same word as Isaac, Abraham's only son
decisions.reason: The word is used of Isaac when God tells Abraham to offer him (Genesis 22:2, 12, 16). There God stops the sacrifice and provides a ram; here no voice from heaven speaks. With an only child, Jephthah's family line also ends.

decisions.choice: not was to him from him son or daughter: he had no child besides her
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "from him", which may mean "of his own": he had no other child of his own. A small change in one letter would give "besides her". Either way the sense is that she was his only child.

decisions.choice: look
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word draws attention to a sudden sight. Literal says "look"; Balanced shows the surprise with "out came"; Readable simply tells what happened.

records.heading: Jephthah's daughter comes out to meet him

records.source: וַיְהִי֩ כִרְאוֹת֨וֹ אוֹתָ֜הּ וַיִּקְרַ֣ע אֶת־בְּגָדָ֗יו וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֲהָ֤הּ בִּתִּי֙ הַכְרֵ֣עַ הִכְרַעְתִּ֔נִי וְאַ֖תְּ הָיִ֣יתְבְּעֹֽכְרָ֑י וְאָנֹכִ֗י פָּצִ֤יתִי־פִי֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֔ה וְלֹ֥א אוּכַ֖ל לָשֽׁוּב׃
records.gloss: And it was when he saw her, and he tore his clothes and said, ah, my daughter! Indeed you have brought me low, and you, you have become among those troubling me; and I, I have opened my mouth to Yahweh, and not I am able to turn back.
pieces: As soon as he saw her, he tore his clothes and cried, "Oh, my daughter! You have struck me down! You have become the one who brings ruin on me. I have given my word to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and I cannot go back on it."

L.35: And it was, when he saw her, that he tore his clothes and said, "Ah, my daughter! You have brought me down utterly, and you have become one of those who trouble me. I have opened my mouth to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and I cannot turn back."

R.35: When Jephthah saw her, he tore his clothes in grief. He cried out, "Oh no, my daughter! You have broken my heart! You have brought terrible trouble on me! I made a promise to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and I cannot take it back."

decisions.choice: he tore his clothes: a sign of deep grief
decisions.reason: Tearing one's clothes showed sorrow or horror (Genesis 37:34; Joshua 7:6).

decisions.choice: those troubling me: the word used of Achan
decisions.reason: The verb means to bring disaster on someone. It is used of Achan, who brought disaster on Israel and was punished in the valley of Achor, "trouble" (Joshua 7:25-26). Jephthah speaks as though his daughter had brought this on him, though the vow was his.

decisions.choice: I have opened my mouth to the LORD: I have made a vow
decisions.reason: To open the mouth to the LORD is to make a vow to him (Psalm 66:14). A vow was to be kept: "he must do all that goes out of his mouth" (Numbers 30:3).

decisions.choice: I cannot turn back: Jephthah believes the vow cannot be undone
decisions.reason: The law let a person vowed to the LORD be redeemed by paying a set price (Leviticus 27:1-8), and a rash oath could be confessed and atoned for (Leviticus 5:4-6). The story does not say whether Jephthah knew of these or sought them.

decisions.choice: struck me down / broken my heart
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the strong doubled verb ("you have utterly brought me low") into plain words of grief.

records.source: וַתֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֗יו אָבִי֙ פָּצִ֤יתָה אֶת־פִּ֨יךָ֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֔ה עֲשֵׂ֣ה לִ֔י כַּאֲשֶׁ֖ר יָצָ֣א מִפִּ֑יךָ אַחֲרֵ֡י אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂה֩ לְךָ֙ יְהוָ֧ה נְקָמ֛וֹת מֵאֹיְבֶ֖יךָ מִבְּנֵ֥י עַמּֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And she said to him, my father, you have opened your mouth to Yahweh; do to me according to what has gone out from your mouth, after that has done for you Yahweh vengeances on your enemies, on [the] sons of Ammon.
pieces: She said to him, "My father, you have given your word to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Do to me what you have promised, now that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has brought justice for you on your enemies the Ammonites."

L.36: And she said to him, "My father, you have opened your mouth to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth, now that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has done acts of vengeance for you on your enemies, on the sons of Ammon."

R.36: She answered, "Father, you made a promise to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. So you must do to me what you said you would. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has punished your enemies, the Ammonites, for you."

decisions.choice: acts of vengeance: the LORD's just punishment of Israel's enemies
decisions.reason: The word is not private revenge but the punishment a ruler or judge gives for a wrong. Jephthah asked the LORD, the Judge, to decide between Israel and Ammon (verse 27); the daughter sees the victory as his verdict.

decisions.choice: do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth: the vow must be kept
decisions.reason: She uses the words of the law on vows (Numbers 30:3) and accepts what her father has promised. She does not ask to be spared, only for time (verse 37).

decisions.choice: brought justice for you on / punished
decisions.reason: "Vengeance" in English often suggests personal revenge; Balanced and Readable use words that keep the sense of just punishment (m1).

records.source: וַתֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל־אָבִ֔יהָ יֵעָ֥שֶׂה לִּ֖י הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה הַרְפֵּ֨ה מִמֶּ֜נִּי שְׁנַ֣יִם חֳדָשִׁ֗ים וְאֵֽלְכָה֙ וְיָרַדְתִּ֣י עַל־הֶֽהָרִ֔ים וְאֶבְכֶּה֙ עַל־בְּתוּלַ֔י אָנֹכִ֖י וְרֵעוֹתָֽי׃
records.gloss: And she said to her father, let be done for me the thing the this: let me alone two months, and I will go and go down upon the mountains and weep over my virginity, I and my companions.
pieces: She also said to her father, "Grant me this one request. Give me two months to go off into the hills with my friends and weep there, because I will never marry."

L.37: And she said to her father, "Let this thing be done for me: let me alone two months, that I may go and go down on the mountains and weep over my virginity, I and my companions."

R.37: Then she said to her father, "Please do this one thing for me. Give me two months to go to the hills with my friends. I want to cry there because I will never get married and have children."

decisions.choice: weep over my virginity: mourn that she will never marry or have children
decisions.reason: The word means the state of a young woman not yet married. To die, or to live, without marrying and bearing children was a great sorrow in Israel, and as an only child she would leave her father no descendants. She mourns what she will never have.

decisions.choice: go down upon the mountains: go off into the hill country
decisions.reason: "Go down" is unusual with "mountains"; it may mean going down from the town into the hill country around it. With one letter different the word would mean "roam", which fits well but is not what the text has.

decisions.choice: my companions: two spellings of one word
decisions.reason: The written text and the marginal reading tradition spell the word for "companions" slightly differently. Both mean her women friends; the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: let me alone: leave me free for a while
decisions.reason: The verb means to let go or hold back. She asks for two months before the vow is carried out.

decisions.choice: weep, because I will never marry
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what weeping over her virginity means (m1); Literal keeps the phrase. They also leave the unusual "go down" as going off into the hills (m2).

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לֵ֔כִי וַיִּשְׁלַ֥ח אוֹתָ֖הּ שְׁנֵ֣י חֳדָשִׁ֑ים וַתֵּ֤לֶךְ הִיא֙ וְרֵ֣עוֹתֶ֔יהָ וַתֵּ֥בְךְּ עַל־בְּתוּלֶ֖יהָ עַל־הֶהָרִֽים׃
records.gloss: And he said, go; and he sent her away two months, and went she and her companions and she wept over her virginity upon the mountains.
pieces: "Go," he said, and he let her go for two months. She went with her friends into the hills and mourned that she would never marry.

L.38: And he said, "Go," and he sent her away [for] two months; and she went, she and her companions, and wept over her virginity on the mountains.

R.38: "Go," he said. He let her go away for two months. She and her friends went to the hills, and she cried because she would never marry.

decisions.choice: wept over her virginity: as in verse 37
decisions.reason: She mourns that she will never marry or have children (verse 37).

decisions.choice: mourned that she would never marry
decisions.reason: As in verse 37.

records.gloss: And it was at [the] end of two months, and she returned to her father, and he did to her his vow that he had vowed; and she not had known a man. And it became a custom in Israel.
pieces: At the end of two months she came back to her father, and he did to her what he had vowed. She had never had relations with a man. And it became a custom in Israel.

L.39: And it was at the end of two months that she returned to her father, and he did to her his vow that he had vowed; and she had not known a man. And it became a custom in Israel.

R.39: After two months she came back to her father, and he did to her what he had promised in his vow. She was still a virgin. And this became a custom in Israel.

decisions.choice: he did to her his vow: he carried out what he had vowed
alternatives: he offered her as a burnt offering
he gave her to the LORD to live unmarried
decisions.reason: The narrator says only that Jephthah did what he had vowed, and the vow said that whoever came out would be the LORD's and be offered as a burnt offering (verse 31). The plain reading is that he put her to death as an offering, a deed the law condemns as the practice of the nations (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31; 18:10; compare 2 Kings 3:27). Another reading holds that she was given to the LORD to live unmarried, perhaps serving at the sanctuary (compare Exodus 38:8; 1 Samuel 2:22). It points to the stress on her virginity in verses 37-39, to the possible "or" in verse 31, and to the lack of any mention of her death. Against it, the vow named a burnt offering, and the mourning and the yearly remembrance suit a death. The story reports the deed without praising it.

decisions.choice: she had not known a man: she had never had sexual relations
decisions.reason: "Know" is a common way of speaking of sexual union (Genesis 4:1). The words say she died, or lived on, without marriage or children (m1).

decisions.choice: it became a custom: the practice of verse 40
decisions.reason: The verb is feminine and could be read "she became an example" in Israel, but most naturally it means "it became a custom", which verse 40 then describes. The word is often used of a fixed law or rule.

decisions.choice: never had relations with a man / was still a virgin
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable avoid the old English use of "know" for sexual union, which modern readers could misread (m2).

decisions.choice: did to her what he had vowed
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the narrator's plain, unexplained words, so that they do not settle the question that m1 leaves open.

records.gloss: From days to days went [the] daughters of Israel to commemorate [the] daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in the year.
pieces: Every year the young women of Israel would go out for four days to commemorate the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite.

L.40: From year to year the daughters of Israel would go to commemorate the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite, four days in the year.

R.40: Each year the young women of Israel went away for four days to tell the story of Jephthah's daughter and to remember her.

decisions.choice: from days to days: year by year
decisions.reason: "Days" can mean a year's time; the phrase means every year, as in 1 Samuel 1:3.

decisions.choice: to commemorate: to tell her story and honor her
decisions.reason: The verb is rare. In 5:11 it means to tell or recount the LORD's deeds, so here it most likely means to retell and remember what happened to her. Some take it as "to lament", which would also suit the yearly gathering.

decisions.choice: went: a repeated, yearly practice
decisions.reason: The verb form describes something done again and again; the custom may still have been kept when the book was written.

decisions.choice: the young women of Israel
decisions.reason: "Daughters of Israel" here means the young women of the people, Jephthah's daughter's companions in age; Literal keeps "daughters".

decisions.choice: to tell the story ... and to remember her
decisions.reason: Readable gives both parts of what commemorating meant (m2).
